mainTopic: A series of aggadic teachings by רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: prayer, names, confronting רשעים, a fixed place for תפילה, and serving a תלמיד חכם.
overview: This amud is mostly a series of teachings by רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי. אברהם was the first to call הקב"ה 'אדון', and רב adds that דניאל's prayer was answered in אברהם's merit. We also learn not to calm a person while he is angry, and that לאה was the first to thank הקב"ה. This leads to explanations of the names ראובן and רות, and to the idea that a name has an effect on a person. Next comes the teaching that a wayward child at home is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג, and why דוד called his flight from אבשלום a 'מזמור'. The גמרא then discusses whether one may confront רשעים and gives several ways to fit the sources together. It closes with the value of a fixed place for תפילה and the teaching that serving a תלמיד חכם is greater than learning from him. Finally, a story about רבי יצחק and רב נחמן leads into another teaching about davening with the צבור, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: אברהם was the first to call God 'Master'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that no one called הקב"ה 'אדון' until אברהם did. The proof is a פסוק in בראשית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: From the day God created the world, no person called Him 'Master' until אברהם came and called Him Master, as it says: 'And he said, My Master, God, how will I know that I will inherit it?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new set of teachings from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי. The first one praises אברהם as the first person to call הקב"ה 'אדון'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim is about history: in all the generations before אברהם, no one addressed הקב"ה as 'Master.' The proof is the word אֲדֹנָי, which אברהם uses when he speaks to הקב"ה in the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Master, Lord: a name that shows God is the master and we are His servants
The Holy One, Blessed be He (God)
In the name of (quoting an earlier teacher)
As it is said: introduces a פסוק as proof

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:

phrases.aramaic: מִיּוֹם שֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: From the day that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created the world,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הָיָה אָדָם שֶׁקְּרָאוֹ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״אָדוֹן״,
phrases.english: there was no person who called the Holy One, Blessed be He, 'Master,'
until Avraham came and called Him Master,
as it is said: 'And he said: My Master, God,'
phrases.notes: בראשית 15:8. The proof is the word אֲדֹנָי, 'my Master.'

phrases.english: 'how will I know that I will inherit it?'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new series of statements by רבי יוחנן, this time in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אברהם was the first person in history to call הקב"ה 'אדון'.

steps.title: דניאל was answered because of אברהם
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that דניאל's prayer was answered only in אברהם's merit. He quotes דניאל's prayer, which ends with the words 'for the sake of אדני'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Even דניאל was answered only because of אברהם, as it says: 'And now, our God, listen to the prayer of Your servant and to his pleas, and shine Your face on Your desolate Temple, for the sake of the Master.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב adds a related teaching about the name 'אדון'. He claims that דניאל's prayer was answered in אברהם's merit and quotes the פסוק he will use as proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on step 1: since אברהם was the one who first called הקב"ה 'אדון', using that name can bring up אברהם's merit. At this point רב has only quoted the פסוק. The next steps explain exactly where the proof is.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of, in the merit of

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: אַף דָּנִיאֵל לֹא נַעֲנָה
phrases.english: Rav said: Even Daniel was not answered
except because of Avraham,
as it is said: 'And now, listen, our God,'
'to the prayer of Your servant and to his pleas,'
'and make Your face shine upon Your desolate Temple,'
'for the sake of the Master.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: אַף דָּנִיאֵל לֹא נַעֲנָה אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל אַבְרָהָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on step 1 by showing a later effect of אברהם calling הקב"ה 'אדון'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דניאל's prayer was accepted in the merit of אברהם.

steps.title: Why doesn't the verse say 'for Your sake'?
steps.stepSummary: רב points out a strange word: דניאל is already talking to הקב"ה, so he should have said 'for Your sake' instead of 'for the sake of אדני'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It should have said 'for Your sake'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that the פסוק's wording is unusual. This sets up the next step, which explains what the wording really means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דניאל speaks to הקב"ה directly ('listen, our God... Your servant... Your face'). Then he suddenly switches to talking about 'the Master,' as if speaking about someone else. That switch tells us the word אֲדֹנָי is hinting at something.

keyTerms.meaning: It should have said (the text should have been worded differently)

phrases.english: It should have said 'for Your sake'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out the extra wording in the פסוק quoted in step 2. This is how רב will prove his claim.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does דניאל say 'for the sake of אדני' instead of 'for Your sake' while he is speaking directly to הקב"ה?

steps.title: For the sake of אברהם, who called You Master
steps.stepSummary: The answer: 'for the sake of אדני' means for the sake of אברהם, the one who first called הקב"ה 'אדון'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means: for the sake of אברהם, who called You 'Master.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 3. דניאל was asking to be answered in the merit of אברהם, the man who first called הקב"ה 'אדון'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אֲדֹנָי points back to the person known for using that name, which is אברהם (step 1). This completes רב's proof that דניאל was answered in אברהם's merit.
steps.whatToRemember: אברהם was the first to call הקב"ה 'אדון'. When דניאל prayed 'for the sake of אדני,' he was asking to be answered in אברהם's merit.

phrases.english: Rather, it means: for the sake of Avraham
who called You 'Master.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 3 and completes רב's proof from step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'אדני' in the פסוק refers to אברהם, who first called הקב"ה 'אדון', so דניאל was asking to be answered in אברהם's merit.

steps.title: Do not try to calm a person while he is angry
steps.stepSummary: Another teaching of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: you should not try to calm someone down while he is still angry. The source is a פסוק in שמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: Where do we learn that we do not try to calm a person while he is angry? As it says: 'My face will go, and then I will give you rest.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from the same pair of רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון בן יוחי. It is about good behavior: do not try to calm a person in the middle of his anger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is הקב"ה's words to משה after the חטא העגל. The גמרא quotes the פסוק here without explaining it. Read simply, first 'My face will go' (the anger passes), and only afterward 'I will give you rest.' So you wait until the anger is over before you try to calm the person.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? (asks for a source)
Appease, try to calm someone or win them over
At the time of his anger, while he is still angry
And I will give rest / calm

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
From where do we know that we do not try to calm a person
while he is angry?
As it is said: 'My face will go, and then I will give you rest.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי: מִנַּיִן שֶׁאֵין מְרַצִּין לוֹ לָאָדָם בִּשְׁעַת כַּעֲסוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching in the same series of רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי. It is not connected to the topic of 'אדון'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should not try to calm a person while he is in the middle of his anger; the source is 'פני ילכו והנחתי לך'.

steps.title: לאה was the first person to thank הקב"ה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that from Creation until לאה, no one had thanked הקב"ה. The proof is what she said when יהודה was born.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן also said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: From the day הקב"ה created His world, no person thanked Him until לאה came and thanked Him. As the פסוק says: 'This time I will thank ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more teaching from the same pair of רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון בן יוחי. This one says לאה was the first person to thank הקב"ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This teaching has the same pattern as the one about אברהם in Step 1: a 'first person who ever did X' line, proven from a פסוק in בראשית. Here the proof is לאה's words when she named יהודה: 'This time I will thank ה׳.'

keyTerms.meaning: this time I will thank (לאה's words when יהודה was born)

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:

phrases.aramaic: מִיּוֹם שֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת עוֹלָמוֹ
phrases.english: From the day the Holy One, Blessed be He, created His world

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הָיָה אָדָם שֶׁהוֹדָה לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: there was no person who thanked the Holy One, Blessed be He,
until Leah came and thanked Him,
as it says: 'This time I will thank God.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 29:35. She says this when naming יהודה.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching from the same רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון בן יוחי series, following the same 'first person to' pattern as Step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לאה was the first person in history to thank הקב"ה, as shown by 'הפעם אודה את ה׳'.

steps.title: The name ראובן: עשו sold his birthright and still hated יעקב
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains the name ראובן as 'ראו בן', 'see the difference between my son and my father-in-law's son.' He begins with עשו, who sold his בכורה willingly but still hated יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The name ראובן: רבי אלעזר said that לאה meant, 'See what a difference there is between my son and my father-in-law's son.' My father-in-law's son, עשו, sold his בכורה by his own choice, as it says, 'He sold his birthright to יעקב.' Yet look what is written about him: 'And עשו hated יעקב.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the גמרא just explained the name יהודה, it now explains the name of לאה's oldest son, ראובן. רבי אלעזר sets up a comparison, and this step gives the first side of it: עשו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name is read as two words: 'ראו', meaning 'see,' and 'בן', meaning 'son.' עשו gave up his בכורה willingly, so he had no fair reason to be angry. Even so, the תורה says he hated יעקב.

keyTerms.meaning: my father-in-law's son (here עשו, son of יצחק)

phrases.english: Reuben.
Rabbi Elazar said:
Leah said: See what the difference is between
phrases.notes: 'רְאוּ' (see) plus 'בֵּן' (son) together make the name רְאוּבֵן.

phrases.english: my son and the son of my father-in-law.
For the son of my father-in-law,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּמִדַּעְתֵּיהּ זַבְּנַיהּ לִבְכֵירוּתֵיהּ,
phrases.english: even though he sold his birthright by his own choice,
as it is written: 'And he sold his birthright to Jacob,'
see what is written about him:
'And Esau hated Jacob.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 6 mentioned the naming of יהודה. This step moves on to explaining the name of another son of לאה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ראובן means 'see the difference': עשו willingly sold his בכורה and still hated יעקב.

steps.title: Proof that עשו was still angry about the birthright
steps.stepSummary: A second פסוק shows that עשו's anger was also about the בכורה he had already sold, and not only about the ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'He said, Is he not rightly named יעקב? He has tricked me twice.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second פסוק to support רבי אלעזר's point. It shows that עשו still complained about losing the בכורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could say עשו hated יעקב only because of the stolen ברכה. Here עשו says he was tricked 'twice,' which counts the בכורה too, even though he sold it by his own choice. So his resentment over the בכורה is proven.

keyTerms.meaning: and it is written (bringing another פסוק)
he tricked me, he went behind my back

phrases.english: And it is written:
'And he said: Is he not rightly called Jacob,'
'for he has tricked me these two times,' etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 7 by showing that עשו's hatred included the בכורה.
steps.raayaObject: עשו resented losing the בכורה even though he sold it willingly.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 27:36, where עשו says יעקב tricked him 'twice.'

steps.title: ראובן lost his birthright by force and still saved יוסף
steps.stepSummary: The other side of the comparison: ראובן's בכורה was taken from him against his will and given to יוסף's sons. Even so, he was not jealous and saved יוסף from his brothers.
steps.simpleTranslation: But my son, even though יוסף took the בכורה from him against his will, as it is written, 'And because he defiled his father's bed, his birthright was given to the sons of יוסף', even so he was not jealous of him. As it is written: 'ראובן heard, and he saved him from their hands.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר finishes the comparison by describing ראובן. He lost far more unfairly than עשו, yet he did not resent יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite of עשו. עשו gave up his בכורה willingly and still hated his brother. ראובן had it taken against his will and still saved the brother who received it. That difference is the 'ראו בן' that לאה pointed to in naming him.

keyTerms.meaning: he was not jealous of him

steps.whatToRemember: ראובן's name means 'see the son.' עשו sold his בכורה willingly and still hated יעקב. ראובן lost his בכורה by force and still saved יוסף.
steps.confusionAlert: The בכורה was not given to יוסף personally. It went to 'the sons of יוסף,' meaning his two sons each became a separate שבט. The גמרא still describes it as יוסף taking it from ראובן.

phrases.english: Whereas my son,
even though against his will
Joseph took his birthright from him,
as it is written: 'And since he defiled his father's bed,'
'his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph,'
even so, he was not jealous of him,
as it is written: 'And Reuben heard, and he saved him from their hands.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the comparison begun in Step 7 by giving the ראובן side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ראובן lost his בכורה by force yet was not jealous, and he saved יוסף. This is the difference between him and עשו that his name points to.

steps.title: The meaning of the name רות
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the name רות hints that דוד, who 'saturated' הקב"ה with songs and praises, would come from her.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does the name רות mean? רבי יוחנן said: she merited that דוד would come from her, and דוד filled up הקב"ה with songs and praises.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the earlier explanation of ראובן's name and now explains the name רות. רבי יוחנן reads it as a hint to her great descendant דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word רות sounds like ריוה, meaning to saturate or give plenty to drink. דוד 'saturated' הקב"ה with שירות ותשבחות in ספר תהלים. So her name already pointed to what would come from her.

keyTerms.meaning: he saturated Him, gave Him plenty (related to the sound of רות)

phrases.english: Ruth, what is the meaning of "Ruth"?
Rabbi Yochanan said:
That she merited that David came from her,
who saturated the Holy One, Blessed be He,
phrases.notes: The word רִיוָּהוּ sounds like רוּת, and that is the hint in her name.

phrases.english: with songs and praises.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of explaining names, which started with ראובן in Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name רות hints that דוד, who saturated הקב"ה with songs and praises, would descend from her.

steps.title: How do we know a name has an effect?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that a person's name actually influences his life.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know that a name has an effect?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask about the idea behind the last few teachings. It is setting up the next step, where רבי אליעזר gives a source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The explanations of ראובן and רות assume that a name tells us something real about a person's future. The גמרא now asks where that assumption comes from.

phrases.english: From where do we know that the name has an effect?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the basis of the name explanations in Steps 7 and 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that a person's name influences his life.

steps.title: Names are among ה׳'s works on earth
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר reads 'שַׁמּוֹת' (desolations) in a פסוק in תהלים as 'שֵׁמוֹת' (names), showing that names are ה׳'s doing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר said: the פסוק says, 'Go, see the works of ה׳, who has placed desolations in the land.' Do not read 'שַׁמּוֹת' (desolations). Read it as 'שֵׁמוֹת' (names).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר answers the question from Step 11 using a פסוק. He changes how one word is read, using an אל תקרי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read the new way, the פסוק says ה׳ 'places names in the land.' So names are among 'the works of ה׳,' and they carry real meaning. That supports the idea that a name affects a person.

keyTerms.meaning: do not read it as..., a way of reading a word differently to learn something

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer said: For the verse says:
"Go, see the works of ה׳,
who has placed desolations in the land."
Do not read it as "shamos" (desolations),
but rather as "shemos" (names).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Names are 'the works of ה׳' that He places in the world, based on reading שַׁמּוֹת as שֵׁמוֹת.
steps.whatToRemember: The name explanations (ראובן, רות) rest on the idea that שמא גרים, a name has an effect. The source is the אל תקרי reading of שַׁמּוֹת as שֵׁמוֹת.

steps.title: A wayward child is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, says that a bad upbringing inside one's own home is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: a wayward child inside a person's house is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching from the same chain, רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי. This is a new topic: trouble at home compared to the great war at the end of days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מלחמת גוג ומגוג is the most terrible war there will be. Even so, the pain of a wayward child in one's own home is described as harder. The proof comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: a bad upbringing; a child who went off the right path
the great war at the end of days

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
A bad upbringing is harder
phrases.notes: Literally 'bad culture.' He means a child who went off the path.

phrases.english: inside a person's house
than the war of Gog and Magog.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching in the series of רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, on a new subject.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wayward child at home is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג.

steps.title: Proof from תהלים chapters 3 and 2
steps.stepSummary: When דוד fled from his son אבשלום he cried 'how many are my enemies.' In the chapter about גוג ומגוג, those words do not appear.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'A song of David, when he fled from Avshalom his son,' and right after it: 'ה׳, how many are my enemies, many rise up against me.' But about the war of גוג ומגוג it says: 'Why are the nations in an uproar, and the peoples speak emptiness.' There, 'how many are my enemies' is not written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the teaching of Step 13 by comparing two chapters of תהלים. One is about דוד running from his son, and the other is about גוג ומגוג.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With אבשלום, דוד cries out in pain: 'how many are my enemies!' In the chapter about גוג ומגוג, the nations' plans are called 'empty,' and there is no cry of distress. So the trouble from his own son weighed on דוד more.

keyTerms.meaning: Absalom, דוד's son who rebelled against him
my enemies, those who trouble me

phrases.english: As it is said: "A song of David,
when he fled from Avshalom his son,"
and it is written after it:
"ה׳, how many are my enemies,
many are rising up against me."

phrases.aramaic: וְאִילּוּ גַּבֵּי מִלְחֶמֶת גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג, כְּתִיב:
phrases.english: Whereas regarding the war of Gog and Magog, it is written:
"Why are the nations in an uproar,
and the peoples speak emptiness?"
phrases.notes: תהלים 2:1. The גמרא reads chapter 2 as being about the war of גוג ומגוג.

phrases.english: But "how many are my enemies" is not written there.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד בְּבָרְחוֹ מִפְּנֵי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the proof for the teaching in Step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That a wayward child at home is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים 3:1-2 ('how many are my enemies,' said about אבשלום) compared with תהלים 2:1, where no such cry appears about גוג ומגוג.
steps.whatToRemember: דוד cried 'מה רבו צרי' over his son אבשלום but not over גוג ומגוג. That shows the pain of a wayward child is harder.

steps.title: Why a song and not a lament?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the chapter about fleeing from אבשלום is called 'מזמור', a song, when it should be called 'קינה', a lament.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A song of David, when he fled from Avshalom his son.' 'A song of David'?! It should have said 'A lament of David'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the opening words of the פסוק it just quoted and points out that they seem strange. This sets up the answer, which comes in steps 16 and 17.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Running away from your own rebellious son is a tragedy, so a 'קינה' (lament) seems to fit. Calling it a 'מזמור' (song of praise) seems to clash with the sad situation. The גמרא wants to know why.

keyTerms.meaning: a song, a psalm of praise
a lament, a sad song of mourning

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question on רבי שמעון בן יוחי's teaching. It is a separate question about the wording of the פסוק, and the answer comes next.

phrases.english: "A song of David, when he fled from Avshalom his son."
"A song of David"?!
It should have said "A lament of David"!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד?! קִינָה לְדָוִד מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the פסוק quoted in Step 14 and questions its opening word.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word 'מזמור' at the start of תהלים 3.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A chapter about fleeing from one's rebellious son is sad, so it should be titled a lament, not a song.

steps.title: The parable of the loan document
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אבישלום answers with a משל. A person who owes a debt is sad before paying it and happy after paying it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אבישלום said: Here is a parable. A man has a loan document against him. Before he pays, he is sad. After he pays, he is happy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins answering why the chapter is called 'מזמור'. It first gives a parable, and the next step will apply it to דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of the parable is that once a feared obligation is finally settled, the worry goes away and relief takes its place. This sets up the idea that a punishment which actually arrives can be a relief compared to the fear of what it might be.

keyTerms.meaning: A loan document showing that someone owes money

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Avishalom said:
A parable: what is this similar to?
To a person against whom a loan document was issued.
Before he paid it, he was sad;
after he paid it, he was happy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the קשיא of step 15 (why 'מזמור' and not 'קינה').
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parable showing relief once a feared debt is settled
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A chapter about running from one's son should be a sad 'קינה'.
steps.terutzMaskana: Relief after a feared outcome is settled can bring joy.

steps.title: Applying the parable to דוד and אבשלום
steps.stepSummary: דוד was told that evil would come from his own house. He feared it would be a slave or a ממזר with no pity. When he saw it was his son אבשלום, he was happy, so he said 'מזמור'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same was true of דוד. When הקדוש ברוך הוא told him, 'I will bring evil against you from your own house,' he was sad. He thought: maybe it will be a slave or a ממזר who will have no pity on me. When he saw it was אבשלום, he was happy. That is why he said 'מזמור'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the parable to דוד and finishes answering the question from step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prophecy was like the debt hanging over דוד. Not knowing who would rise against him was the frightening part. Once he saw it was his own son, who he expected would have mercy, the 'debt' was paid in the gentlest way, so he sang a song instead of a lament.

keyTerms.meaning: I will raise up evil against you from your own house
A child born from a forbidden relationship

steps.whatToRemember: דוד said 'מזמור' because his punishment came through his own son, who would have mercy on him, and not through a stranger with no pity.

phrases.english: So too with David:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: when the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him:
"Behold, I will raise up evil against you from your own house,"
he was sad. He said:
Perhaps it will be a slave or a mamzer,
who will have no pity on me.
Once he saw that it was Avshalom, he was happy.
That is why he said "a song."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the parable from step 16 to דוד.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing the event as relief rather than tragedy
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fleeing from his son was pure tragedy, so it should be a 'קינה'.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was relief, because the feared punishment came through a son who would have pity, so it is a 'מזמור'.

steps.title: It is permitted to stand up against the wicked
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, says it is permitted to confront רשעים in this world, based on a פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: It is permitted to stand up against wicked people in this world, as it says: 'Those who leave the תורה praise the wicked, and those who keep the תורה fight against them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from the same pair, רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, about confronting wicked people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק contrasts two groups. People who abandon the תורה praise the wicked, while people who keep the תורה fight them. So fighting the wicked is the way of תורה-keepers, and it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: To provoke, to stand up against

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
It is permitted to stand up against wicked people in this world,
as it is said:
"Those who abandon the Torah praise the wicked one,
and those who keep the Torah fight against them."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching in the series of statements by רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי (like step 13).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is permitted to confront the wicked in this world.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the same thing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports the teaching with a ברייתא in which רבי דוסתאי ברבי מתון says the same rule from the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was also taught in a ברייתא. רבי דוסתאי ברבי מתון says: It is permitted to stand up against wicked people in this world, as it says: 'Those who leave the תורה praise the wicked,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that an older teaching, a ברייתא, says the same thing as רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'תניא נמי הכי' means a ברייתא agrees. Here an earlier source teaches the same rule from the same פסוק, which strengthens רבי יוחנן's statement. The ברייתא will also go on to deal with a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא
And so on (the rest of the פסוק)

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Matun says:
It is permitted to stand up against wicked people in this world,
as it is said: "Those who abandon the Torah praise the wicked one," and so on.
phrases.notes: The rest of the פסוק, 'and those who keep the תורה fight against them,' is the key part.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 18 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that one may confront the wicked in this world
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי דוסתאי ברבי מתון

steps.title: A פסוק that seems to say not to fight the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises a challenge. A פסוק in תהלים says 'do not compete with evildoers,' which seems to forbid confronting them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if a person whispers to you: But it is written, 'Do not compete with evildoers, do not be jealous of those who do wrong.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a פסוק that seems to contradict the rule that one may fight the wicked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Do not compete with evildoers' sounds like a command to stay away from fights with wicked people. That seems to clash directly with the פסוק in משלי that says תורה-keepers fight them.

phrases.english: And if a person whispers to you, saying:
But isn't it written:
"Do not compete with evildoers,
do not be jealous of those who do wrong"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם לְחָשְׁךָ אָדָם לוֹמַר: וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule taught in steps 18-19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that one may confront the wicked
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק in תהלים seems to forbid quarreling with evildoers, contradicting the פסוק in משלי.

steps.title: The פסוק means: do not become like the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that only someone with a guilty conscience reads the פסוק that way. It really means: do not compete to be like the evildoers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Tell him: Only someone whose heart bothers him says that. Rather, 'do not compete with evildoers' means do not try to be like the evildoers, and 'do not be jealous of those who do wrong' means do not try to be like those who do wrong.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the challenge by explaining what the פסוק in תהלים really means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The questioner read 'do not compete' as 'do not fight them.' The ברייתא reads it as 'do not envy them and copy their ways.' So the פסוק warns against becoming wicked and says nothing against confronting the wicked, and the rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose heart bothers him, a guilty conscience

steps.whatToRemember: It is permitted to stand up against the wicked. The פסוק 'אל תתחר במרעים' only forbids envying them and copying their ways.

phrases.english: Say to him:
Only one whose heart bothers him says this.
Rather, "do not compete with evildoers" means:
to be like the evildoers;
"do not be jealous of those who do wrong" means:
to be like those who do wrong.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֱמוֹר לוֹ: מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ נוֹקְפוֹ אוֹמֵר כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 20.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Do not compete with evildoers' means do not confront them.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means do not envy them or try to be like them, so confronting them is still permitted.

steps.title: A second פסוק shows the right meaning of 'do not compete'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings a פסוק from משלי to support its reading: 'do not compete' means do not try to be like the sinners.
steps.simpleTranslation: And another פסוק says: 'Let your heart not envy sinners, but rather be in fear of ה׳ all day.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a second פסוק to back up its answer from the last step. The פסוק shows that the warning is about not envying sinners and becoming like them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 21 the ברייתא said 'do not compete with evildoers' means 'do not try to be like them.' This פסוק says the same idea openly: do not envy sinners, but fear ה׳ instead. So the warning is about copying רשעים, not about confronting them.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it says': brings an additional פסוק as more support
to envy, or to compete with

phrases.english: And it says: 'Let your heart not envy sinners,'

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אִם בְּיִרְאַת ה׳ כָּל הַיּוֹם״.
phrases.english: but rather be in fear of ה׳ all day.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second פסוק that supports the ברייתא's answer in step 21
steps.raayaObject: The reading that 'do not compete with evildoers' means 'do not try to be like them'

steps.title: רבי יצחק says not to provoke a successful רשע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule that one may confront רשעים. רבי יצחק says not to provoke a רשע while things are going well for him, and he proves it from three parts of a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? Didn't רבי יצחק say: If you see a wicked person who is having good fortune, do not provoke him. As it says, 'His ways prosper at all times.' And not only that, he even wins in judgment, as it says, 'Your judgments are far beyond him.' And not only that, he even sees the downfall of his enemies, as it says, 'All his foes, he snorts at them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the teaching that it is permitted to confront רשעים. It brings רבי יצחק, who warns against provoking a רשע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן and the ברייתא said one may confront רשעים. רבי יצחק says not to provoke a רשע who is having good fortune, because his success will continue. He bases this on three parts of one פסוק: the רשע succeeds, he wins in judgment, and he sees his enemies fall.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But didn't he say?': brings a teaching that contradicts what was just said
the hour is smiling on him; he is having good fortune
and not only that, but also

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But didn't רבי יצחק say:
If you see a wicked person
upon whom the hour is smiling,
do not provoke him,
as it says: 'His ways prosper at all times.'
And not only that, but he wins in judgment,
as it says: 'Your judgments are far beyond him.'
And not only that, but he sees the downfall of his enemies,
as it says: 'All his foes, he snorts at them!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule from steps 18-22 that it is permitted to confront רשעים
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's teaching, in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי, together with the ברייתא, that it is permitted to confront רשעים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יצחק forbids provoking a רשע who is having good fortune, which seems to contradict permission to confront רשעים

steps.title: Personal matters versus matters of Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The first answer: רבי יצחק is talking about personal matters, and the permission to confront is about matters of Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This teaching (do not provoke) is about his own personal matters. That teaching (you may confront) is about matters of Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by saying the two teachings are about different kinds of situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Do not pick a fight with a successful רשע over your own personal interests. When the issue is a matter of Heaven, such as his wrongdoing against the תורה, you may confront him. So the two teachings do not clash.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult; there is no contradiction
this one... that one: sorts two sources into two different cases

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is about his own personal matters,
phrases.notes: 'This' means רבי יצחק's warning not to provoke the רשע.

phrases.english: that is about matters of Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from step 23
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by subject matter
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both teachings seemed to speak about the same situation, so they contradicted each other
steps.terutzMaskana: Do not provoke a רשע over personal matters. You may confront him over matters of Heaven.

steps.title: Second answer: is the רשע having good fortune or not?
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: both teachings are about matters of Heaven. רבי יצחק means a רשע who is having good fortune, and the permission to confront means a רשע who is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say that both teachings are about matters of Heaven, and it is still not difficult. This one is about a wicked person who is having good fortune. That one is about a wicked person who is not having good fortune.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the same contradiction. This time it divides the cases by the רשע's situation, not by the subject.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even in matters of Heaven, do not confront a רשע while things are going well for him, since רבי יצחק's פסוק says his success continues. When his luck is not with him, you may confront him. This answer fits the words of רבי יצחק's own teaching, which mentions a רשע 'upon whom the hour is smiling.'

keyTerms.meaning: and if you want, say: introduces a second, alternative answer
the hour is not smiling on him; he is not having good fortune

steps.whatToRemember: Two ways to fit the teachings together: (1) personal matters, do not provoke; matters of Heaven, you may confront. (2) Even in matters of Heaven, do not provoke a רשע who is having good fortune; you may confront one who is not.

phrases.english: And if you want, say
this and that are both about matters of Heaven,
and it is not difficult:
this is about a wicked person upon whom the hour is smiling,

phrases.aramaic: הָא בְּרָשָׁע שֶׁאֵין הַשָּׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ.
phrases.english: that is about a wicked person upon whom the hour is not smiling.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא הָא וְהָא בְּמִילֵּי דִשְׁמַיָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different answer to the קשיא from step 23, instead of the answer in step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the רשע's situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the only way to fit the teachings together is to split personal matters from matters of Heaven
steps.terutzMaskana: Even in matters of Heaven, do not provoke a רשע who is having good fortune. You may confront one who is not.

steps.title: A third answer: it depends on who is confronting
steps.stepSummary: Both teachings are about a רשע whose luck is good. A צדיק גמור may confront him; a צדיק who is not complete may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: both teachings are about a wicked person whose hour is smiling on him. Still, there is no contradiction. The permission to confront is for a completely righteous person. The warning not to confront is for a righteous person who is not complete.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third way to settle the clash between רבי יצחק (do not provoke a successful רשע) and the permission to confront רשעים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 25 split the cases by the רשע: is he lucky or not? This answer agrees that the רשע is lucky in both cases. Instead it splits the cases by the person confronting him: is he a צדיק גמור or not?

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces another possible answer
The hour is smiling on him: he is having good fortune
And it is not difficult: there is no contradiction

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: הָא וְהָא, בְּרָשָׁע שֶׁהַשָּׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ,
phrases.english: this and that are both about a wicked person on whom the hour is smiling,
phrases.notes: "This and that" means רבי יצחק's warning and the teaching that you may confront רשעים.

phrases.english: and it is not difficult:
this is about a completely righteous person,
that is about a righteous person who is not complete.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא, בְּרָשָׁע שֶׁהַשָּׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third, alternative answer to the קשיא of step 23, after the answers in steps 24 and 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the person who confronts (צדיק גמור vs. not complete)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two teachings seem to argue about confronting a successful רשע.
steps.terutzMaskana: A צדיק גמור may confront even a successful רשע. A less-than-complete צדיק should not.

steps.title: רב הונא quotes a פסוק from חבקוק
steps.stepSummary: To support the third answer, the גמרא brings רב הונא, who asks about a פסוק that says the רשע swallows one more righteous than he.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא said: What does this פסוק mean: "Why do You look at traitors and stay silent when the wicked swallows one more righteous than he?"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a proof from רב הונא. This step quotes the פסוק and gets ready to ask a question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "more righteous than he" will turn out to be the key. They hint that the victim is only somewhat righteous, not a צדיק גמור.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written

phrases.english: As Rav Huna said:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"Why do You look at traitors and keep silent
when the wicked swallows one more righteous than he?"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for the third answer in step 26.
steps.raayaObject: That a less-than-complete צדיק can be harmed by a רשע, but a צדיק גמור cannot
steps.raayaSupportSource: חבקוק 1:13 as explained by רב הונא

steps.title: Can a רשע really swallow a צדיק?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא asks how the פסוק can say a רשע swallows a צדיק, when other פסוקים say ה׳ protects the צדיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does a wicked person really swallow a righteous one? But it is written: "ה׳ will not leave him in his hand." And it is written: "No harm shall befall the righteous."
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא challenges the simple reading of the פסוק in חבקוק. He points to two other פסוקים that say a צדיק is protected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in חבקוק seems to say a צדיק can be destroyed. תהלים and משלי say the צדיק is safe. This contradiction needs an answer, and the answer will support step 26.

keyTerms.meaning: And is it so that...? (a surprised question)
But it is written: brings a פסוק that contradicts

phrases.english: Does a wicked person really swallow a righteous one?
But it is written:
"ה׳ will not leave him in his hand,"
phrases.notes: תהלים 37:33. "Him" is the צדיק, and "his hand" is the רשע's hand.

phrases.english: and it is written:
"No harm shall befall the righteous."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי רָשָׁע בּוֹלֵעַ צַדִּיק? וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the פסוק quoted in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of חבקוק 1:13, that a רשע swallows a צדיק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Other פסוקים say ה׳ never lets the צדיק fall into the רשע's hand.

steps.title: Only a צדיק who is not complete can be swallowed
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers: the רשע swallows someone only 'more righteous than he', but not a צדיק גמור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: one who is only more righteous than him, he swallows. A completely righteous person he does not swallow.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא settles the contradiction by reading the words "more righteous than he" carefully.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in חבקוק is about a person who is only better than the רשע, not a צדיק גמור. The other פסוקים are about the צדיק גמור, who is protected. This supports step 26: a צדיק גמור may confront a רשע, but a lesser צדיק could get hurt.

keyTerms.meaning: More righteous than he: only better than the רשע, not fully righteous

steps.whatToRemember: A צדיק גמור is protected from the רשע, so he may confront him. A less-than-complete צדיק is not fully protected.

phrases.english: Rather:
one who is only more righteous than him, he swallows;
a completely righteous person, he does not swallow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 28 and finishes the proof for step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Careful reading of the wording ("more righteous than he")
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seems to say any צדיק can be swallowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a partly righteous person can be swallowed. A צדיק גמור is protected.

steps.title: Another answer: good fortune changes things
steps.stepSummary: Another way to settle the פסוקים: normally a רשע cannot swallow a צדיק, but when the רשע's hour is smiling, it is different.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: when the hour is smiling on him, it is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to settle the contradiction between חבקוק and the other פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the difference is the רשע's luck, not how righteous the victim is. When the רשע's luck is good, even a צדיק can be harmed. When it is not, the צדיק is protected.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
when the hour is smiling on him, it is different.
phrases.notes: "Him" is the רשע. When his luck is good, he can harm even a צדיק.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, שָׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ — שָׁאנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An alternative answer to the contradiction raised in step 28, in place of step 29's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the רשע's fortune
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוקים contradict about whether a רשע can harm a צדיק.
steps.terutzMaskana: A רשע with good fortune can harm a צדיק. Otherwise he cannot.

steps.title: A fixed place for תפילה makes enemies fall
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that whoever sets a fixed place for his תפילה sees his enemies fall beneath him. He proves it from a פסוק in שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: Whoever sets a fixed place for his prayer, his enemies fall beneath him. As it says: "I will set a place for My people Israel and plant them, and they will dwell in their place, and be disturbed no more, and the wicked will no longer afflict them as before."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new teaching from the same pair of rabbis: the value of a fixed place for davening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof uses the word "place" (מקום) in the פסוק. It ties that place to the promise that enemies will no longer afflict Israel. So a set place leads to protection from enemies.

keyTerms.meaning: One who sets a fixed place
As it is said: introduces a פסוק as proof

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practice of having a set place to daven.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:
Whoever sets a fixed place for his prayer,
his enemies fall beneath him.
As it is said:
"And I will set a place for My people Israel,
and I will plant them, and they will dwell in their place,
and they will be disturbed no more,
and the wicked will no longer afflict them
as at first."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching from the same pair of rabbis, unrelated to confronting רשעים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setting a fixed place for תפילה brings protection from enemies.

steps.title: Two פסוקים, two different words
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא points out that this פסוק says 'to afflict them', but the parallel פסוק says 'to destroy them'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא pointed out a contradiction: It is written "to afflict them," and it is written "to destroy them."
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא raises a contradiction between two versions of the same promise. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל says the wicked will no longer 'afflict' Israel. The same promise in דברי הימים says 'destroy'. The גמרא must explain why the wording differs.

keyTerms.meaning: Raised a contradiction (literally, threw against each other)

phrases.english: Rav Huna pointed out a contradiction:
it is written "to afflict them,"
and it is written "to destroy them."
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א 17:9, the same promise told again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the פסוק quoted in step 31 and notes how its wording differs from a parallel פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of שמואל ב 7:10 compared with דברי הימים א 17:9
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two versions of the same promise use different verbs: 'afflict' and 'destroy'.

steps.title: First afflict, then destroy
steps.stepSummary: The two פסוקים don't contradict: the enemy wants first to afflict Israel and in the end to wipe them out.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first, to afflict him; and in the end, to destroy him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב הונא's question from the last step by showing that each פסוק describes a different stage of the enemy's plan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One פסוק says 'to afflict' and the parallel פסוק says 'to destroy.' The answer is that both are true, one after the other: the enemy starts with oppression, and his final goal is destruction. So the two פסוקים describe one plan at two points in time.
steps.whatToRemember: Two פסוקים that seem to clash can describe two stages of the same event: first affliction, then the attempt to destroy.

phrases.english: At first — to afflict him,
and in the end — to destroy him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב הונא's contradiction between 'to afflict' and 'to destroy.'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting by time: each פסוק describes a different stage.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two פסוקים describe the enemy's intent differently and seem to contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: The enemy starts by afflicting and ends by trying to destroy, so both words are accurate.

steps.title: Serving a תלמיד חכם is greater than learning from him
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that serving Torah is greater than studying it. He proves it from אלישע pouring water on אליהו's hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: Serving Torah is greater than learning it. As it says: 'Here is אלישע son of שפט, who poured water on the hands of אליהו.' It does not say 'learned,' it says 'poured.' This teaches that serving Torah is greater than learning it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching from the same chain, רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי. This one says that serving a תלמיד חכם is even greater than learning from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from how the פסוק praises אלישע. It does not describe him as אליהו's student who learned from him. It describes him as the one who poured water on his hands, meaning he served him. Since the פסוק picked serving as his claim to greatness, serving must be greater than learning.

keyTerms.meaning: serving Torah, meaning personally attending a תלמיד חכם
it does not say X, rather it says Y (a reading drawn from the exact word choice)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that being close to a תלמיד חכם and watching how he lives teaches things that book learning alone cannot.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:

phrases.aramaic: גְּדוֹלָה שִׁמּוּשָׁהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה יוֹתֵר מִלִּמּוּדָהּ,
phrases.english: Greater is the service of Torah than its study,
phrases.notes: 'Service of Torah' means personally serving a תלמיד חכם and spending time with him.

phrases.english: as it says: 'Here is Elisha son of Shafat,'

phrases.aramaic: אֲשֶׁר יָצַק מַיִם עַל יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ״.
phrases.english: 'who poured water on the hands of Elijah.'
It does not say 'learned,' rather 'poured' —
this teaches that its service is greater than its study.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, unrelated teaching in the series of רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, which runs through this amud from step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Serving a תלמיד חכם is greater than learning Torah from him, as shown by the פסוק praising אלישע for pouring water for אליהו.

steps.title: Why didn't you come to shul to daven?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק asks רב נחמן why he did not come to the בית כנסת to daven.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said to רב נחמן: Why didn't the Master come to the בית כנסת to daven?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story that leads into another teaching of רבי יוחנן. רבי יצחק asks רב נחמן why he skipped davening in shul.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story sets the stage. רבי יצחק clearly thinks davening with the צבור in shul matters a great deal. The reason for that is revealed at the end of this story.

keyTerms.meaning: 'the Master,' a respectful way of saying 'you'

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִצְחָק לְרַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said to Rav Nachman:
Why did the Master not come
to the synagogue to pray?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָתֵי מָר לְבֵי כְּנִישְׁתָּא לְצַלּוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story that serves as a lead-in to another teaching of רבי יוחנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב נחמן did not come to the בית כנסת to daven.

steps.title: I wasn't able to
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that he was unable to come.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I was not able.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן explains that he could not make it to shul.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He gives a simple reason: he was not able to come, probably from weakness. This sets up רבי יצחק's search for another way for him to daven with a group.

keyTerms.meaning: I am not able, I could not

phrases.english: He said to him: I was not able.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יצחק's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He was not able to come to the בית כנסת.

steps.title: Gather a מנין at home? Too much bother
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק suggests gathering ten men at home to daven; רב נחמן says that would be too much of a burden.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Let the Master gather ten people and daven. He said to him: It is a burden for me.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק offers a first solution, a מנין at רב נחמן's home, and רב נחמן turns it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he cannot come to the צבור, the צבור could come to him. רב נחמן rejects this because troubling ten people to come to his house is too heavy a burden. So רבי יצחק needs a different idea.

keyTerms.meaning: the matter is a burden for me

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לִכַּנְפִי לְמָר עַשְׂרָה וְלִיצַלֵּי.
phrases.english: He said to him: Let the Master gather ten and pray.
He said to him: The matter is burdensome for me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a way around רב נחמן's inability to come, which רב נחמן rejects.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea of a home מנין.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Bringing ten people to his house would be too great a burden.

steps.title: Have a messenger tell you when the צבור davens
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק suggests that רב נחמן arrange for a messenger to let him know when the צבור is davening, so he can daven at the same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: And let the Master tell the צבור's messenger: at the time the צבור davens, let him come and tell the Master.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק offers a second solution. If רב נחמן can't come and can't bring a מנין home, he can at least daven at the same time as the צבור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This idea costs no one any real trouble. רב נחמן stays home but davens at the exact time the צבור is davening. This shows how much רבי יצחק cares about davening together with the צבור.

phrases.english: And let the Master tell the messenger of the congregation,
phrases.notes: This line has no 'he said to him,' so רבי יצחק is still the one speaking.

phrases.english: that at the time the congregation is praying
he should come and inform the Master.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the home מנין is rejected, רבי יצחק offers a lighter option.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A practical fix that avoids the burden of the earlier idea.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If he can't go to shul or gather ten, there is no way to connect his davening to the צבור.
steps.terutzMaskana: He can daven at the same time as the צבור by being told when they daven.

steps.title: Why all this effort?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks why רבי יצחק is pushing so hard. רבי יצחק begins his answer by quoting רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What is all this for? He said to him: Because רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי:
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן asks why it matters so much, and רבי יצחק starts to answer with a teaching. This is a setup line: the actual teaching comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole story was building to this point. רבי יצחק's push to have רב נחמן daven with the צבור, or at least at the same time, is based on a teaching of רבי יוחנן. We have to wait for the next line to hear what it says.
steps.confusionAlert: The teaching itself is not on this amud. The line ends right after the name רבי שמעון בן יוחי, and his words continue on the next amud.

phrases.english: He said to him: What is all this for?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: He said to him: Because Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the suggestions, רב נחמן asks for the reason behind them, and רבי יצחק begins to explain.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יצחק is so determined that רב נחמן daven together with the צבור.
